Empirical Research Plan  
“Price Reactions to Quarterly Earnings Announcements in the Dow Jones Industrial Index, 1989-1993”

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  

Chosen method: Short-horizon event study (a special case of interrupted-time-series/DID in which the “interruption” is known to the minute and the pre-period supplies the counterfactual).  

Justification  
• The research question concerns the immediate causal effect of a precisely-timed information shock (the earnings release) on equity values.  
• We observe high-frequency outcome data (daily returns) and can cleanly separate a narrow post-announcement window from a long pre-announcement estimation window to infer normal (counterfactual) returns.  
• Because the shock is unanticipated in sign and size, the Efficient Market Hypothesis implies any valuation effect should show up in abnormal returns tightly clustered around the event.  
• Relative to alternatives (DID, IV, RDD) an event study uses the same firm’s pre-announcement return process as its own control, thereby eliminating time-invariant firm characteristics and most time-varying market-wide shocks (via the market model).  

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
T_iq = categorical variable for announcement i in quarter q:  
 GoodNews = 1{ (Actual − Forecast)/|Forecast| > +2.5% }  
 BadNews  = 1{ (Actual − Forecast)/|Forecast| < −2.5% }  
 NoNews   = base category (|Actual − Forecast| ≤ 2.5%).  

Control / counterfactual  
The normal daily return predicted by the market model estimated over the 250-day [−270, −21] window before each announcement.  

Treatment timing / event date  
t = 0 is the Datastream announcement date. We examine abnormal returns from t = −20 … +20 and calculate cumulative abnormal return (CAR) in a primary window of [−1, +1] trading days.  

(There is no RDD running variable, nor an IV.)  

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Market efficiency at the daily horizon  
 Prices fully and quickly reflect public information; hence any price change inside the short window is caused by the announcement.  
 Plausibility: Well-accepted in the large earnings-response literature; five-day or shorter windows are a standard.  

A2. No confounding firm-specific news in the event window  
 No other material information releases (e.g., M&A, dividend changes) that systematically coincide with earnings releases.  
 Plausibility: Firms tend to bundle some news with earnings, but we can check major news wires and drop contaminated observations.  

A3. Stable return-generating process in estimation window  
 The parameters α_i, β_i of the market model are constant between the estimation window and the event window.  
 Plausibility: 250 prior days is conventional; we can test for structural breaks.  

A4. Announcement-date accuracy and no leak/lag outside window  
 The recorded Datastream date matches the first public dissemination, and information leakage earlier than −1 is minimal.  
 Plausibility: US disclosure rules require prompt filing; still, we will look for pre-trend abnormal returns to verify.  

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

Threat 1: Bundled or confounding news  
 Mitigation: Manually search Factiva/Lexis for other events; drop or flag contaminated announcements; run robustness excluding ±1 day if needed.  

Threat 2: Information leakage or delayed market reaction  
 Mitigation: Inspect abnormal returns in [−10, −2] and [+2, +10]; if significant, shorten window or expand it symmetrically and attribute only the instantaneous jump to the announcement.  

Threat 3: Estimation-window parameter instability (β drift)  
 Mitigation: (i) Use alternative expected-return models: market-adjusted, Fama-French 3-factor. (ii) Re-estimate α_i, β_i on rolling 120-day windows as robustness.  

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(zoo)

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
earn  <- fread("earnings_announcements.csv")   # firm_id, ann_date, actual_eps, exp_eps
prices<- fread("daily_returns.csv")            # firm_id, date, ret
mkt   <- fread("market_returns.csv")           # date, mkt_ret

# 2. Merge and create treatment dummies ------------------------------------
earn[, surprise := (actual_eps - exp_eps)/abs(exp_eps)]
earn[, `:=`(Good = (surprise >  0.025),
            Bad  = (surprise < -0.025))]
earn[, No := !(Good | Bad)]   # implicit
earn[, ann_date := as.Date(ann_date)]

# 3. Create event-time daily panel -----------------------------------------
setkey(prices, firm_id, date)
setkey(earn,  firm_id, ann_date)

# join prices within [-270, +20]
window <- 270+20
eventDT <- earn[, {
  start <- ann_date-270
  end   <- ann_date+20
  prices[.(firm_id)][date >= start & date <= end,
         .(date, ret, evt_time = as.integer(date - ann_date))]
}, by = .(firm_id, ann_date, Good, Bad)]

# merge market returns
setkey(mkt, date)
eventDT <- mkt[eventDT]

# 4. Estimate market model parameters --------------------------------------
est_params <- eventDT[evt_time %between% c(-270, -21),
   {
     fit <- lm(ret ~ mkt_ret)
     .(alpha = coef(fit)[1], beta = coef(fit)[2])
   }, by = .(firm_id, ann_date)]

eventDT <- est_params[eventDT, on = .(firm_id, ann_date)]
eventDT[, abn_ret := ret - alpha - beta*mkt_ret]

# 5. Compute Cumulative Abnormal Return (CAR) ------------------------------
car <- eventDT[evt_time %between% c(-1, +1),
     .(CAR = sum(abn_ret)), by = .(firm_id, ann_date, Good, Bad)]

# 6. Regression: impact of earnings surprise category ----------------------
car[, Bad := as.numeric(Bad); Good := as.numeric(Good)]  # factors → 0/1
main_mod <- feols(CAR ~ Good + Bad | firm_id, data = car,
                  cluster = ~firm_id)
summary(main_mod)

# 7. Robustness: alternative window [-20,+20] ------------------------------
car20 <- eventDT[evt_time %between% c(-20, +20),
  .(CAR20 = sum(abn_ret)), by = .(firm_id, ann_date, Good, Bad)]
rob_mod <- feols(CAR20 ~ Good + Bad | firm_id, data = car20,
                 cluster = ~firm_id)
summary(rob_mod)
```
(The code can be extended to use `tidyquant` for Fama-French factors and to perform placebo tests using pseudo-event dates.)  

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Economic theory (and decades of earnings-response work) predicts:  
• Good news ⇒ positive CAR, roughly +2% to +4% over [−1,+1].  
• Bad news ⇒ negative CAR, roughly −3% to −5%.  
• No news ⇒ CAR statistically indistinguishable from zero.  
Magnitude asymmetry (|Bad| > |Good|) is plausible due to loss-aversion and differential attention.  

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event Study)  

C1: Precise dating of the event ............... 1  
C2: Window free of other confounding events ... 0.8  
C3: No pre-trend / leakage outside window ..... 0.8  
C4: Stable return-generating process .......... 0.9  
C5: Correct inference (clustering, thin-tails)  1  

Overall ≈ 4.5 / 5 – design is strong but contingent on careful event screening and leakage tests.
